# RTBO Academy University - Complete College Course Manual
## Ultimate Deep-Dive Training Program for Basketball Officials

### Purpose
This is the full student-facing course packet for RTBO Academy University. It is written as the material a student-official receives on the first day of class. It does not operate like a short clinic outline. It functions like a college program with daily lectures, laboratories, written assignments, oral defenses, film work, mechanics practicums, mentor conferences, examinations, and graduation requirements. Each track is written as a 12-month academic path. Every week contains seven academic days. Every day contains line items with professor-level explanation, student performance requirements, and measurable expected outcomes.

### Source and Rulebook Foundation
The program is built as an officiating education framework and should be paired each season with the current official rulebooks, casebooks, mechanics manuals, league/conference directives, supervisor bulletins, and points of emphasis for the governing body being served. The curriculum references NCAA men’s and women’s rulebook availability through NCAA Publications, NBA official rulebook and officiating resources through NBA Official, and professional replay/officials structures through the NBA official rules architecture. Students must always study the current year’s official rulebook and local conference interpretations before applying this curriculum to live games.

### Daily Academic Expectations
Students report daily with a rulebook, mechanics notebook, film journal, whistle, court shoes, and the current module worksheet. Students are expected to write every day, speak every day, analyze film every week, perform mechanics every week, and defend rulings orally. Attendance alone does not create progress. Progress is earned through demonstrated competence.

### Degree Progression
Bachelor-level tracks establish collegiate foundation. Master-level tracks develop advanced collegiate performance. Doctoral-level tracks prepare officials for elite professional-style reasoning, leadership, analytics, replay awareness, and public-pressure environments. Completion of any track does not certify an official for a league by itself; it documents RTBO Academy training, evaluation, and readiness for appropriate assignments or advancement consideration.


# SCHOOL / TRACK: NJCAA WOMEN
## Degree Path: Bachelor of Science in Basketball Officiating - Collegiate Foundation Track
## Academic Level: Bachelor Year 1 / Associate-to-Bachelor Bridge

### Track Identity
This track is designed for junior-college women’s basketball officials preparing to manage developing collegiate athletes, diverse gym environments, quick roster turnover, and freedom-of-movement responsibilities. Students in this track study the full annual officiating cycle through classroom lecture, court mechanics, film laboratory, role-play, live practicum, mentoring, written exams, oral defense, and advancement board review. The teaching emphasis throughout the year is to teach fairness, safety, and disciplined communication in the junior-college women’s game.

### Graduation Requirements for This Track
- Complete all 52 weeks of daily academic work.
- Pass all written rules and philosophy examinations.
- Complete every film-lab assignment and full-game self-scout.
- Demonstrate mechanics competence in two-person and three-person systems appropriate to the track.
- Complete role-play scenarios involving coaches, players, partners, table crew, observers, and supervisors.
- Submit required reports for technical, flagrant, administrative, spectator, facility, and unusual situations applicable to the track.
- Complete live-practicum observations and receive mentor/evaluator approval.
- Defend final portfolio before the RTBO advancement board.


## Month 1, Week 1: Orientation and Professional Identity
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NJCAA Women program is devoted to Orientation and Professional Identity. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of professional identity, service to the game, academic expectations, and the student-official’s first personal development contract. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NJCAA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism, developmental college environment, shot-clock awareness, player safety, mentor-driven growth. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Orientation and Professional Identity affects the NJCAA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.


### Week 1, Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar
#### Line Item 1 - Professor Explanation
The instructional line for NJCAA Women Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar in Week 1 is that orientation and professional identity must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to junior-college women’s basketball officials preparing to manage developing collegiate athletes, diverse gym environments, quick roster turnover, and freedom-of-movement responsibilities. The student is expected to understand that professional identity, service to the game, academic expectations, and the student-official’s first personal development contract directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism influence the way this lesson appears in the NJCAA Women environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student performs the day’s work as follows: The professor introduces the week’s thesis, teaches the governing philosophy, questions the students orally, and requires every student to explain how the concept affects real officiating decisions. For the NJCAA Women pathway, that performance must be connected to teach fairness, safety, and disciplined communication in the junior-college women’s game. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, intentional-contact concepts where applicable by adopted rule set, disqualifying behavior, and reportable unsporting acts. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Orientation and Professional Identity. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to junior-college women’s basketball officials preparing to manage developing collegiate athletes, diverse gym environments, quick roster turnover, and freedom-of-movement responsibilities. The student is expected to understand that live-ball status, dead-ball status, player control, team control, frontcourt and backcourt status, and the rule logic that controls rulings directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism influence the way this lesson appears in the NJCAA Women environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 2 - Rules, Case Plays, and Written Reasoning, the student performs the day’s work as follows: Students work through rule language, case-play logic, penalty administration, and written explanations that require precision rather than guesswork. For the NJCAA Women pathway, that performance must be connected to teach fairness, safety, and disciplined communication in the junior-college women’s game. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, intentional-contact concepts where applicable by adopted rule set, disqualifying behavior, and reportable unsporting acts. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

The expected outcome for this line is measurable. ## Month 1, Week 3: Mechanics as Visual Science
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NJCAA Women program is devoted to Mechanics as Visual Science. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of open angles, closed angles, primary coverage, movement discipline, Lead/Center/Trail visual responsibilities, and the connection between mechanics and judgment. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NJCAA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism, developmental college environment, shot-clock awareness, player safety, mentor-driven growth. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Mechanics as Visual Science affects the NJCAA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 1, Week 4: Communication Psychology
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NJCAA Women program is devoted to Communication Psychology. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of tone, timing, posture, coach dialogue, player dialogue, table communication, and emotional discipline. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NJCAA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism, developmental college environment, shot-clock awareness, player safety, mentor-driven growth. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Communication Psychology affects the NJCAA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 2, Week 7: Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NJCAA Women program is devoted to Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of rhythm, speed, balance, quickness, displacement, freedom of movement, and game-flow judgment. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NJCAA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism, developmental college environment, shot-clock awareness, player safety, mentor-driven growth. ## Month 2, Week 8: Technical and Reportable Conduct
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NJCAA Women program is devoted to Technical and Reportable Conduct. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of technical fouls, bench decorum, unsporting conduct, excessive contact, flagrant-style conduct, and professional report writing. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NJCAA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism, developmental college environment, shot-clock awareness, player safety, mentor-driven growth. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of Lead/Center/Trail structure, rotations, strong-side and weak-side responsibilities, secondary coverage, and crew discipline. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NJCAA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism, developmental college environment, shot-clock awareness, player safety, mentor-driven growth. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Three-Person Mechanics Laboratory affects the NJCAA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.


### Week 10, Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar
#### Line Item 1 - Professor Explanation
The instructional line for NJCAA Women Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar in Week 10 is that three-person mechanics laboratory must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to junior-college women’s basketball officials preparing to manage developing collegiate athletes, diverse gym environments, quick roster turnover, and freedom-of-movement responsibilities. The student is expected to understand that Lead/Center/Trail structure, rotations, strong-side and weak-side responsibilities, secondary coverage, and crew discipline directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism influence the way this lesson appears in the NJCAA Women environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. For the NJCAA Women pathway, that performance must be connected to teach fairness, safety, and disciplined communication in the junior-college women’s game. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, intentional-contact concepts where applicable by adopted rule set, disqualifying behavior, and reportable unsporting acts. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. The instructional line for NJCAA Women Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar in Week 23 is that full-game film review must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to junior-college women’s basketball officials preparing to manage developing collegiate athletes, diverse gym environments, quick roster turnover, and freedom-of-movement responsibilities. The student is expected to understand that building a complete game evaluation, identifying performance patterns, fatigue trends, and development priorities directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism influence the way this lesson appears in the NJCAA Women environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student performs the day’s work as follows: The professor introduces the week’s thesis, teaches the governing philosophy, questions the students orally, and requires every student to explain how the concept affects real officiating decisions. For the NJCAA Women pathway, that performance must be connected to teach fairness, safety, and disciplined communication in the junior-college women’s game. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, intentional-contact concepts where applicable by adopted rule set, disqualifying behavior, and reportable unsporting acts. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Full-Game Film Review. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

## Month 8, Week 30: Level-Specific Game Management Intensive

This week in the NJCAA Women program is devoted to Level-Specific Game Management Intensive. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of coach behavior, player behavior, bench decorum, rivalry pressure, and league/conference communication expectations. ## Month 11, Week 42: Elite Contact Judgment
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NJCAA Women program is devoted to Elite Contact Judgment. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of marginal contact, illegal displacement, high-speed advantage, post contact, transition contact, and late-game foul selection. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NJCAA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to women’s game pace, perimeter freedom of movement, emotional intelligence, bench professionalism, developmental college environment, shot-clock awareness, player safety, mentor-driven growth. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Elite Contact Judgment affects the NJCAA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

# FINAL CAPSTONE FOR NJCAA WOMEN
The final capstone for NJCAA Women requires a complete officiating portfolio. The student submits full-year journals, rules exams, mechanics rubrics, film analysis, live observations, mentor notes, report-writing samples, communication role-play scores, and a personal advancement statement. During the final oral defense, the student must explain how they would manage a difficult game in the NJCAA Women environment, including pregame preparation, crew communication, contact philosophy, coach management, serious foul reporting, film self-scouting, and postgame professionalism. The board may ask the student to explain rules, justify a call/no-call, review a film clip, defend a report, or describe how they would handle a supervisor’s criticism. Passing the capstone earns RTBO Academy completion for this track and places the student into an assignment or advancement category based on demonstrated evidence.


# SCHOOL / TRACK: NJCAA MEN
## Degree Path: Bachelor of Science in Basketball Officiating - Collegiate Foundation Track
## Academic Level: Bachelor Year 1 / Associate-to-Bachelor Bridge

### Track Identity
This track is designed for junior-college men’s basketball officials preparing for pace, physicality, transition contact, emotional bench behavior, and rapid player development. Students in this track study the full annual officiating cycle through classroom lecture, court mechanics, film laboratory, role-play, live practicum, mentoring, written exams, oral defense, and advancement board review. The teaching emphasis throughout the year is to balance physical play, game flow, and player safety in the junior-college men’s environment.

### Graduation Requirements for This Track
- Complete all 52 weeks of daily academic work.
- Pass all written rules and philosophy examinations.
- Complete every film-lab assignment and full-game self-scout.
- Demonstrate mechanics competence in two-person and three-person systems appropriate to the track.
- Complete role-play scenarios involving coaches, players, partners, table crew, observers, and supervisors.
- Submit required reports for technical, flagrant, administrative, spectator, facility, and unusual situations applicable to the track.
- Complete live-practicum observations and receive mentor/evaluator approval.
- Defend final portfolio before the RTBO advancement board.

## Month 1, Week 3: Mechanics as Visual Science
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NJCAA Men program is devoted to Mechanics as Visual Science. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of open angles, closed angles, primary coverage, movement discipline, Lead/Center/Trail visual responsibilities, and the connection between mechanics and judgment. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NJCAA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to men’s junior-college physicality, transition officiating, post play, rebounding displacement, coach management, bench control, competitive temperature, assignment reliability. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Mechanics as Visual Science affects the NJCAA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 2, Week 7: Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NJCAA Men program is devoted to Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of rhythm, speed, balance, quickness, displacement, freedom of movement, and game-flow judgment. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NJCAA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to men’s junior-college physicality, transition officiating, post play, rebounding displacement, coach management, bench control, competitive temperature, assignment reliability. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy affects the NJCAA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 8, Week 30: Level-Specific Game Management Intensive

This week in the NJCAA Men program is devoted to Level-Specific Game Management Intensive. The instructional line for NJCAA Men Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance in Week 40 is that teaching clinics and court stations must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to junior-college men’s basketball officials preparing for pace, physicality, transition contact, emotional bench behavior, and rapid player development. The student is expected to understand that clinic design, station rotation, classroom delivery, film-room leadership, and adult-learning principles directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how men’s junior-college physicality, transition officiating, post play, rebounding displacement influence the way this lesson appears in the NJCAA Men environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance, the student performs the day’s work as follows: Students perform the concept on the court through movement, positioning, whistle, signal, and crew-communication laboratories. For the NJCAA Men pathway, that performance must be connected to balance physical play, game flow, and player safety in the junior-college men’s environment. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, excessive contact, unsporting acts, intentional/flagrant-style contact review by adopted rule set, and postgame incident reporting. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Teaching Clinics and Court Stations. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

## Month 11, Week 42: Elite Contact Judgment
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NJCAA Men program is devoted to Elite Contact Judgment. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of marginal contact, illegal displacement, high-speed advantage, post contact, transition contact, and late-game foul selection. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NJCAA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to men’s junior-college physicality, transition officiating, post play, rebounding displacement, coach management, bench control, competitive temperature, assignment reliability. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Elite Contact Judgment affects the NJCAA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

# FINAL CAPSTONE FOR NJCAA MEN
The final capstone for NJCAA Men requires a complete officiating portfolio. The student submits full-year journals, rules exams, mechanics rubrics, film analysis, live observations, mentor notes, report-writing samples, communication role-play scores, and a personal advancement statement. During the final oral defense, the student must explain how they would manage a difficult game in the NJCAA Men environment, including pregame preparation, crew communication, contact philosophy, coach management, serious foul reporting, film self-scouting, and postgame professionalism. The board may ask the student to explain rules, justify a call/no-call, review a film clip, defend a report, or describe how they would handle a supervisor’s criticism. Passing the capstone earns RTBO Academy completion for this track and places the student into an assignment or advancement category based on demonstrated evidence.


# SCHOOL / TRACK: NAIA WOMEN
## Degree Path: Master of Science in Collegiate Basketball Officiating - Small College Women’s Concentration
## Academic Level: Master Year 1

### Track Identity
This track is designed for small-college women’s basketball officials preparing for national tournament environments, advanced crew communication, travel professionalism, and supervisor-ready film review. Students in this track study the full annual officiating cycle through classroom lecture, court mechanics, film laboratory, role-play, live practicum, mentoring, written exams, oral defense, and advancement board review. The teaching emphasis throughout the year is to develop professional small-college women’s officials who can handle championship pressure with composure.

### Graduation Requirements for This Track
- Complete all 52 weeks of daily academic work.
- Pass all written rules and philosophy examinations.
- Complete every film-lab assignment and full-game self-scout.
- Demonstrate mechanics competence in two-person and three-person systems appropriate to the track.
- Complete role-play scenarios involving coaches, players, partners, table crew, observers, and supervisors.
- Submit required reports for technical, flagrant, administrative, spectator, facility, and unusual situations applicable to the track.
- Complete live-practicum observations and receive mentor/evaluator approval.
- Defend final portfolio before the RTBO advancement board.


## Month 1, Week 1: Orientation and Professional Identity
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Women program is devoted to Orientation and Professional Identity. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of professional identity, service to the game, academic expectations, and the student-official’s first personal development contract. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure, crew trust, travel professionalism, supervisor feedback, advanced film self-scouting. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Orientation and Professional Identity affects the NAIA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 1, Week 2: Rules Architecture and Definitions
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Women program is devoted to Rules Architecture and Definitions. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of live-ball status, dead-ball status, player control, team control, frontcourt and backcourt status, and the rule logic that controls rulings. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure, crew trust, travel professionalism, supervisor feedback, advanced film self-scouting. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Rules Architecture and Definitions affects the NAIA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 1, Week 3: Mechanics as Visual Science
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Women program is devoted to Mechanics as Visual Science. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of open angles, closed angles, primary coverage, movement discipline, Lead/Center/Trail visual responsibilities, and the connection between mechanics and judgment. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure, crew trust, travel professionalism, supervisor feedback, advanced film self-scouting. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

## Month 2, Week 6: Foul Theory and Contact Classification
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Women program is devoted to Foul Theory and Contact Classification. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of common fouls, shooting fouls, player-control, team-control, illegal contact, marginal contact, and contact that affects the play. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure, crew trust, travel professionalism, supervisor feedback, advanced film self-scouting. ## Month 2, Week 7: Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Women program is devoted to Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of rhythm, speed, balance, quickness, displacement, freedom of movement, and game-flow judgment. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure, crew trust, travel professionalism, supervisor feedback, advanced film self-scouting. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy affects the NAIA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 3, Week 11: Transition, Press Coverage, and Fast-Break Judgment
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Women program is devoted to Transition, Press Coverage, and Fast-Break Judgment. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of backcourt pressure, traps, long passes, secondary defenders, transition contact, and fast-break rulings. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure, crew trust, travel professionalism, supervisor feedback, advanced film self-scouting. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of short preventive phrases, emotional player management, unsporting behavior prevention, and respect without familiarity. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure, crew trust, travel professionalism, supervisor feedback, advanced film self-scouting. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Player Communication and Preventive Officiating affects the NAIA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.


### Week 17, Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar
#### Line Item 1 - Professor Explanation
The instructional line for NAIA Women Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar in Week 17 is that player communication and preventive officiating must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to small-college women’s basketball officials preparing for national tournament environments, advanced crew communication, travel professionalism, and supervisor-ready film review. The student is expected to understand that short preventive phrases, emotional player management, unsporting behavior prevention, and respect without familiarity directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure influence the way this lesson appears in the NAIA Women environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student performs the day’s work as follows: The professor introduces the week’s thesis, teaches the governing philosophy, questions the students orally, and requires every student to explain how the concept affects real officiating decisions. For the NAIA Women pathway, that performance must be connected to develop professional small-college women’s officials who can handle championship pressure with composure. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, unsporting conduct, excessive contact, flagrant-style review concepts by governing rule set, and tournament-level reporting. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Player Communication and Preventive Officiating. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

## Month 5, Week 20: Film Study Methodology
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Women program is devoted to Film Study Methodology. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of how to watch film as an official, primary coverage identification, play sequencing, and evidence-based self-scouting. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure, crew trust, travel professionalism, supervisor feedback, advanced film self-scouting. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Film Study Methodology affects the NAIA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 6, Week 24: Evaluation Preparation
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Women program is devoted to Evaluation Preparation. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of understanding evaluation rubrics, receiving feedback, preparing for observation, and self-assessing before formal grading. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure, crew trust, travel professionalism, supervisor feedback, advanced film self-scouting. The instructional line for NAIA Women Day 2 - Rules, Case Plays, and Written Reasoning in Week 30 is that level-specific game management intensive must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to small-college women’s basketball officials preparing for national tournament environments, advanced crew communication, travel professionalism, and supervisor-ready film review. The student is expected to understand that coach behavior, player behavior, bench decorum, rivalry pressure, and league/conference communication expectations directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure influence the way this lesson appears in the NAIA Women environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 2 - Rules, Case Plays, and Written Reasoning, the student performs the day’s work as follows: Students work through rule language, case-play logic, penalty administration, and written explanations that require precision rather than guesswork. For the NAIA Women pathway, that performance must be connected to develop professional small-college women’s officials who can handle championship pressure with composure. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, unsporting conduct, excessive contact, flagrant-style review concepts by governing rule set, and tournament-level reporting. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 2 - Rules, Case Plays, and Written Reasoning, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Level-Specific Game Management Intensive. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

The instructional line for NAIA Women Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar in Week 42 is that elite contact judgment must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to small-college women’s basketball officials preparing for national tournament environments, advanced crew communication, travel professionalism, and supervisor-ready film review. The student is expected to understand that marginal contact, illegal displacement, high-speed advantage, post contact, transition contact, and late-game foul selection directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure influence the way this lesson appears in the NAIA Women environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student performs the day’s work as follows: The professor introduces the week’s thesis, teaches the governing philosophy, questions the students orally, and requires every student to explain how the concept affects real officiating decisions. For the NAIA Women pathway, that performance must be connected to develop professional small-college women’s officials who can handle championship pressure with composure. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, unsporting conduct, excessive contact, flagrant-style review concepts by governing rule set, and tournament-level reporting. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Elite Contact Judgment. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

This week in the NAIA Women program is devoted to Final Mechanics Examination. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of court mechanics practical, video review of positioning, movement correction, and final mechanics rubric. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure, crew trust, travel professionalism, supervisor feedback, advanced film self-scouting. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Final Mechanics Examination affects the NAIA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.


### Week 46, Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar
#### Line Item 1 - Professor Explanation
The instructional line for NAIA Women Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar in Week 46 is that final mechanics examination must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to small-college women’s basketball officials preparing for national tournament environments, advanced crew communication, travel professionalism, and supervisor-ready film review. The student is expected to understand that court mechanics practical, video review of positioning, movement correction, and final mechanics rubric directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how NAIA women’s championship culture, advanced three-person mechanics, freedom of movement, postseason pressure influence the way this lesson appears in the NAIA Women environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student performs the day’s work as follows: The professor introduces the week’s thesis, teaches the governing philosophy, questions the students orally, and requires every student to explain how the concept affects real officiating decisions. For the NAIA Women pathway, that performance must be connected to develop professional small-college women’s officials who can handle championship pressure with composure. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, unsporting conduct, excessive contact, flagrant-style review concepts by governing rule set, and tournament-level reporting. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Final Mechanics Examination. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

# FINAL CAPSTONE FOR NAIA WOMEN
The final capstone for NAIA Women requires a complete officiating portfolio. The student submits full-year journals, rules exams, mechanics rubrics, film analysis, live observations, mentor notes, report-writing samples, communication role-play scores, and a personal advancement statement. During the final oral defense, the student must explain how they would manage a difficult game in the NAIA Women environment, including pregame preparation, crew communication, contact philosophy, coach management, serious foul reporting, film self-scouting, and postgame professionalism. The board may ask the student to explain rules, justify a call/no-call, review a film clip, defend a report, or describe how they would handle a supervisor’s criticism. Passing the capstone earns RTBO Academy completion for this track and places the student into an assignment or advancement category based on demonstrated evidence.


# SCHOOL / TRACK: NAIA MEN
## Degree Path: Master of Science in Collegiate Basketball Officiating - Small College Men’s Concentration
## Academic Level: Master Year 1

### Track Identity
This track is designed for small-college men’s basketball officials preparing for high physicality, national tournament intensity, advanced post play, and mature game management. Students in this track study the full annual officiating cycle through classroom lecture, court mechanics, film laboratory, role-play, live practicum, mentoring, written exams, oral defense, and advancement board review. The teaching emphasis throughout the year is to train officials to manage small-college men’s basketball without over-officiating or losing safety standards.

### Graduation Requirements for This Track
- Complete all 52 weeks of daily academic work.
- Pass all written rules and philosophy examinations.
- Complete every film-lab assignment and full-game self-scout.
- Demonstrate mechanics competence in two-person and three-person systems appropriate to the track.
- Complete role-play scenarios involving coaches, players, partners, table crew, observers, and supervisors.
- Submit required reports for technical, flagrant, administrative, spectator, facility, and unusual situations applicable to the track.
- Complete live-practicum observations and receive mentor/evaluator approval.
- Defend final portfolio before the RTBO advancement board.


## Month 1, Week 1: Orientation and Professional Identity
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Men program is devoted to Orientation and Professional Identity. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of professional identity, service to the game, academic expectations, and the student-official’s first personal development contract. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact, advanced advantage-disadvantage, crew-chief leadership, postseason readiness, supervisor-style evaluation. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Orientation and Professional Identity affects the NAIA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

The student is expected to understand that professional identity, service to the game, academic expectations, and the student-official’s first personal development contract directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact influence the way this lesson appears in the NAIA Men environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 7 - Reflection, Remediation, Mentor Conference, and Advancement Record, the student performs the day’s work as follows: Students complete written reflection, remediation tasks, mentor conference notes, and dashboard updates documenting growth and next steps. For the NAIA Men pathway, that performance must be connected to train officials to manage small-college men’s basketball without over-officiating or losing safety standards. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, unsporting acts, excessive-contact situations, flagrant-style concepts by adopted rule set, and crew-chief incident reporting. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

The expected outcome for this line is measurable. ## Month 1, Week 2: Rules Architecture and Definitions
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Men program is devoted to Rules Architecture and Definitions. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of live-ball status, dead-ball status, player control, team control, frontcourt and backcourt status, and the rule logic that controls rulings. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact, advanced advantage-disadvantage, crew-chief leadership, postseason readiness, supervisor-style evaluation. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Rules Architecture and Definitions affects the NAIA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 1, Week 4: Communication Psychology

This week in the NAIA Men program is devoted to Communication Psychology. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of tone, timing, posture, coach dialogue, player dialogue, table communication, and emotional discipline. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact, advanced advantage-disadvantage, crew-chief leadership, postseason readiness, supervisor-style evaluation. ## Month 2, Week 5: Violations and Administrative Precision
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Men program is devoted to Violations and Administrative Precision. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of traveling, illegal dribble, backcourt, out-of-bounds, substitutions, timeouts, timing corrections, and administrative reliability. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact, advanced advantage-disadvantage, crew-chief leadership, postseason readiness, supervisor-style evaluation. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Violations and Administrative Precision affects the NAIA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 2, Week 6: Foul Theory and Contact Classification
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Men program is devoted to Foul Theory and Contact Classification. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of common fouls, shooting fouls, player-control, team-control, illegal contact, marginal contact, and contact that affects the play. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact, advanced advantage-disadvantage, crew-chief leadership, postseason readiness, supervisor-style evaluation. ## Month 3, Week 9: Two-Person Mechanics Laboratory
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Men program is devoted to Two-Person Mechanics Laboratory. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of Lead and Trail responsibilities, transition coverage, throw-ins, free throws, rebounding, and last-second shot responsibility. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact, advanced advantage-disadvantage, crew-chief leadership, postseason readiness, supervisor-style evaluation. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Two-Person Mechanics Laboratory affects the NAIA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 3, Week 10: Three-Person Mechanics Laboratory
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Men program is devoted to Three-Person Mechanics Laboratory. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of Lead/Center/Trail structure, rotations, strong-side and weak-side responsibilities, secondary coverage, and crew discipline. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact, advanced advantage-disadvantage, crew-chief leadership, postseason readiness, supervisor-style evaluation. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Three-Person Mechanics Laboratory affects the NAIA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 6, Week 22: Self-Scouting Judgment
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Men program is devoted to Self-Scouting Judgment. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of reviewing personal call/no-call decisions, contact evaluation, patient whistle timing, and philosophical consistency. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact, advanced advantage-disadvantage, crew-chief leadership, postseason readiness, supervisor-style evaluation.
