## Month 10, Week 39: Evaluation Writing
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Men program is devoted to Evaluation Writing. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of balanced feedback, strengths, areas for improvement, examples, recommendations, and avoiding vague criticism. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact, advanced advantage-disadvantage, crew-chief leadership, postseason readiness, supervisor-style evaluation. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Evaluation Writing affects the NAIA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 11, Week 42: Elite Contact Judgment
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NAIA Men program is devoted to Elite Contact Judgment. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of marginal contact, illegal displacement, high-speed advantage, post contact, transition contact, and late-game foul selection. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NAIA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact, advanced advantage-disadvantage, crew-chief leadership, postseason readiness, supervisor-style evaluation. The instructional line for NAIA Men Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance in Week 50 is that advancement board review must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to small-college men’s basketball officials preparing for high physicality, national tournament intensity, advanced post play, and mature game management. The student is expected to understand that panel defense, evidence review, leadership questions, score verification, and placement decision directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how NAIA men’s physicality, elite post play, competitive benches, rebounding contact influence the way this lesson appears in the NAIA Men environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance, the student performs the day’s work as follows: Students perform the concept on the court through movement, positioning, whistle, signal, and crew-communication laboratories. For the NAIA Men pathway, that performance must be connected to train officials to manage small-college men’s basketball without over-officiating or losing safety standards. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, unsporting acts, excessive-contact situations, flagrant-style concepts by adopted rule set, and crew-chief incident reporting. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Advancement Board Review. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.


### Week 52 Closing Conference
At the end of Week 52, the professor, mentor, or evaluator meets with the student to review all submitted evidence. The student must explain what changed in their thinking, what action they performed, what error they corrected, and what remains unfinished. For the NAIA Men track, the conference specifically asks how the week’s material supports train officials to manage small-college men’s basketball without over-officiating or losing safety standards. The student’s record is marked complete only when written work, lab work, film work, role-play, and practicum evidence are all submitted.


# FINAL CAPSTONE FOR NAIA MEN
The final capstone for NAIA Men requires a complete officiating portfolio. The student submits full-year journals, rules exams, mechanics rubrics, film analysis, live observations, mentor notes, report-writing samples, communication role-play scores, and a personal advancement statement. During the final oral defense, the student must explain how they would manage a difficult game in the NAIA Men environment, including pregame preparation, crew communication, contact philosophy, coach management, serious foul reporting, film self-scouting, and postgame professionalism. The board may ask the student to explain rules, justify a call/no-call, review a film clip, defend a report, or describe how they would handle a supervisor’s criticism. Passing the capstone earns RTBO Academy completion for this track and places the student into an assignment or advancement category based on demonstrated evidence.


# SCHOOL / TRACK: NCAA WOMEN
## Degree Path: Master of Science in Elite Basketball Officiating - NCAA Women’s Concentration
## Academic Level: Master Year 2 / NCAA Development

### Track Identity
This track is designed for NCAA women’s basketball officials preparing for national standards, advanced mechanics, freedom of movement, replay awareness, F1/F2 concepts, and supervisor accountability. Students in this track study the full annual officiating cycle through classroom lecture, court mechanics, film laboratory, role-play, live practicum, mentoring, written exams, oral defense, and advancement board review. The teaching emphasis throughout the year is to produce NCAA women’s officials capable of accurate, composed, nationally consistent officiating.

### Graduation Requirements for This Track
- Complete all 52 weeks of daily academic work.
- Pass all written rules and philosophy examinations.
- Complete every film-lab assignment and full-game self-scout.
- Demonstrate mechanics competence in two-person and three-person systems appropriate to the track.
- Complete role-play scenarios involving coaches, players, partners, table crew, observers, and supervisors.
- Submit required reports for technical, flagrant, administrative, spectator, facility, and unusual situations applicable to the track.
- Complete live-practicum observations and receive mentor/evaluator approval.
- Defend final portfolio before the RTBO advancement board.


## Month 1, Week 1: Orientation and Professional Identity
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NCAA Women program is devoted to Orientation and Professional Identity. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of professional identity, service to the game, academic expectations, and the student-official’s first personal development contract. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NCAA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NCAA women’s rules philosophy, advanced freedom of movement, Flagrant 1 analysis, Flagrant 2 analysis, shot-clock and game-clock administration, coach communication, endgame review, supervisor-ready performance. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Orientation and Professional Identity affects the NCAA Women environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

#### Line Item 1 - Professor Explanation

This week in the NCAA Women program is devoted to Mechanics as Visual Science. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of open angles, closed angles, primary coverage, movement discipline, Lead/Center/Trail visual responsibilities, and the connection between mechanics and judgment. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NCAA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NCAA women’s rules philosophy, advanced freedom of movement, Flagrant 1 analysis, Flagrant 2 analysis, shot-clock and game-clock administration, coach communication, endgame review, supervisor-ready performance. ## Month 1, Week 4: Communication Psychology
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NCAA Women program is devoted to Communication Psychology. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of tone, timing, posture, coach dialogue, player dialogue, table communication, and emotional discipline. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NCAA Women pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NCAA women’s rules philosophy, advanced freedom of movement, Flagrant 1 analysis, Flagrant 2 analysis, shot-clock and game-clock administration, coach communication, endgame review, supervisor-ready performance. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

# FINAL CAPSTONE FOR NCAA WOMEN
The final capstone for NCAA Women requires a complete officiating portfolio. The student submits full-year journals, rules exams, mechanics rubrics, film analysis, live observations, mentor notes, report-writing samples, communication role-play scores, and a personal advancement statement. During the final oral defense, the student must explain how they would manage a difficult game in the NCAA Women environment, including pregame preparation, crew communication, contact philosophy, coach management, serious foul reporting, film self-scouting, and postgame professionalism. The board may ask the student to explain rules, justify a call/no-call, review a film clip, defend a report, or describe how they would handle a supervisor’s criticism. Passing the capstone earns RTBO Academy completion for this track and places the student into an assignment or advancement category based on demonstrated evidence.


# SCHOOL / TRACK: NCAA MEN
## Degree Path: Master of Science in Elite Basketball Officiating - NCAA Men’s Concentration
## Academic Level: Master Year 2 / NCAA Development

### Track Identity
This track is designed for NCAA men’s basketball officials preparing for advanced physicality, Class A and Class B technicals, F1/F2 evaluation, monitor awareness, and high-pressure coach communication. Students in this track study the full annual officiating cycle through classroom lecture, court mechanics, film laboratory, role-play, live practicum, mentoring, written exams, oral defense, and advancement board review. The teaching emphasis throughout the year is to prepare NCAA men’s officials for high-speed, high-pressure, supervisor-evaluated collegiate basketball.

### Graduation Requirements for This Track
- Complete all 52 weeks of daily academic work.
- Pass all written rules and philosophy examinations.
- Complete every film-lab assignment and full-game self-scout.
- Demonstrate mechanics competence in two-person and three-person systems appropriate to the track.
- Complete role-play scenarios involving coaches, players, partners, table crew, observers, and supervisors.
- Submit required reports for technical, flagrant, administrative, spectator, facility, and unusual situations applicable to the track.
- Complete live-practicum observations and receive mentor/evaluator approval.
- Defend final portfolio before the RTBO advancement board.


## Month 1, Week 1: Orientation and Professional Identity
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NCAA Men program is devoted to Orientation and Professional Identity. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of professional identity, service to the game, academic expectations, and the student-official’s first personal development contract. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NCAA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NCAA men’s physicality, Class A technical foul judgment, Class B technical foul administration, Flagrant 1 analysis, Flagrant 2 analysis, monitor awareness, restricted-area judgment, late-game credibility. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Orientation and Professional Identity affects the NCAA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 2, Week 5: Violations and Administrative Precision
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NCAA Men program is devoted to Violations and Administrative Precision. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of traveling, illegal dribble, backcourt, out-of-bounds, substitutions, timeouts, timing corrections, and administrative reliability. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NCAA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NCAA men’s physicality, Class A technical foul judgment, Class B technical foul administration, Flagrant 1 analysis, Flagrant 2 analysis, monitor awareness, restricted-area judgment, late-game credibility. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Violations and Administrative Precision affects the NCAA Men environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 2, Week 6: Foul Theory and Contact Classification
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NCAA Men program is devoted to Foul Theory and Contact Classification. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of common fouls, shooting fouls, player-control, team-control, illegal contact, marginal contact, and contact that affects the play. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NCAA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NCAA men’s physicality, Class A technical foul judgment, Class B technical foul administration, Flagrant 1 analysis, Flagrant 2 analysis, monitor awareness, restricted-area judgment, late-game credibility. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

## Month 4, Week 14: Post Play, Rebounding, and Screening
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NCAA Men program is devoted to Post Play, Rebounding, and Screening. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of post displacement, legal verticality, rebounding contact, illegal screens, off-ball coverage, and matchup awareness. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NCAA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NCAA men’s physicality, Class A technical foul judgment, Class B technical foul administration, Flagrant 1 analysis, Flagrant 2 analysis, monitor awareness, restricted-area judgment, late-game credibility. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

## Month 7, Week 28: Level-Specific Rules Intensive
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NCAA Men program is devoted to Level-Specific Rules Intensive. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of rule-set differences, adopted interpretations, foul categories, clock rules, reporting terminology, and governing-level expectations. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NCAA Men pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NCAA men’s physicality, Class A technical foul judgment, Class B technical foul administration, Flagrant 1 analysis, Flagrant 2 analysis, monitor awareness, restricted-area judgment, late-game credibility. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

# FINAL CAPSTONE FOR NCAA MEN
The final capstone for NCAA Men requires a complete officiating portfolio. The student submits full-year journals, rules exams, mechanics rubrics, film analysis, live observations, mentor notes, report-writing samples, communication role-play scores, and a personal advancement statement. During the final oral defense, the student must explain how they would manage a difficult game in the NCAA Men environment, including pregame preparation, crew communication, contact philosophy, coach management, serious foul reporting, film self-scouting, and postgame professionalism. The board may ask the student to explain rules, justify a call/no-call, review a film clip, defend a report, or describe how they would handle a supervisor’s criticism. Passing the capstone earns RTBO Academy completion for this track and places the student into an assignment or advancement category based on demonstrated evidence.


# SCHOOL / TRACK: WNBA
## Degree Path: Doctor of Professional Basketball Officiating - WNBA Development Concentration
## Academic Level: Doctoral Professional Residency

### Track Identity
This track is designed for elite professional women’s basketball officials preparing for public scrutiny, professional player communication, replay culture, national broadcast pressure, and advanced consistency demands. Students in this track study the full annual officiating cycle through classroom lecture, court mechanics, film laboratory, role-play, live practicum, mentoring, written exams, oral defense, and advancement board review. The teaching emphasis throughout the year is to build professional women’s basketball officials with elite communication, accuracy, and public-pressure discipline.

### Graduation Requirements for This Track
- Complete all 52 weeks of daily academic work.
- Pass all written rules and philosophy examinations.
- Complete every film-lab assignment and full-game self-scout.
- Demonstrate mechanics competence in two-person and three-person systems appropriate to the track.
- Complete role-play scenarios involving coaches, players, partners, table crew, observers, and supervisors.
- Submit required reports for technical, flagrant, administrative, spectator, facility, and unusual situations applicable to the track.
- Complete live-practicum observations and receive mentor/evaluator approval.
- Defend final portfolio before the RTBO advancement board.


## Month 1, Week 1: Orientation and Professional Identity
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the WNBA program is devoted to Orientation and Professional Identity. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of professional identity, service to the game, academic expectations, and the student-official’s first personal development contract. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the WNBA pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to professional women’s game, elite player communication, broadcast pressure, replay awareness, public accountability, player safety, professional game flow, championship crew discipline. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Orientation and Professional Identity affects the WNBA environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

## Month 1, Week 2: Rules Architecture and Definitions
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the WNBA program is devoted to Rules Architecture and Definitions. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of live-ball status, dead-ball status, player control, team control, frontcourt and backcourt status, and the rule logic that controls rulings. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the WNBA pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to professional women’s game, elite player communication, broadcast pressure, replay awareness, public accountability, player safety, professional game flow, championship crew discipline. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Rules Architecture and Definitions affects the WNBA environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

This week in the WNBA program is devoted to Foul Theory and Contact Classification. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the WNBA pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to professional women’s game, elite player communication, broadcast pressure, replay awareness, public accountability, player safety, professional game flow, championship crew discipline. # FINAL CAPSTONE FOR WNBA
The final capstone for WNBA requires a complete officiating portfolio. The student submits full-year journals, rules exams, mechanics rubrics, film analysis, live observations, mentor notes, report-writing samples, communication role-play scores, and a personal advancement statement. During the final oral defense, the student must explain how they would manage a difficult game in the WNBA environment, including pregame preparation, crew communication, contact philosophy, coach management, serious foul reporting, film self-scouting, and postgame professionalism. The board may ask the student to explain rules, justify a call/no-call, review a film clip, defend a report, or describe how they would handle a supervisor’s criticism. Passing the capstone earns RTBO Academy completion for this track and places the student into an assignment or advancement category based on demonstrated evidence.


# SCHOOL / TRACK: NBA
## Degree Path: Doctor of Professional Basketball Officiating - NBA Elite Concentration
## Academic Level: Doctoral Professional Residency

### Track Identity
This track is designed for elite professional basketball officials preparing for NBA-style rule administration, Replay Center interaction, Coach’s Challenge procedures, professional crew hierarchy, and national-level performance analytics. Students in this track study the full annual officiating cycle through classroom lecture, court mechanics, film laboratory, role-play, live practicum, mentoring, written exams, oral defense, and advancement board review. The teaching emphasis throughout the year is to develop officials who think, prepare, communicate, and self-scout like elite professional basketball officials.

### Graduation Requirements for This Track
- Complete all 52 weeks of daily academic work.
- Pass all written rules and philosophy examinations.
- Complete every film-lab assignment and full-game self-scout.
- Demonstrate mechanics competence in two-person and three-person systems appropriate to the track.
- Complete role-play scenarios involving coaches, players, partners, table crew, observers, and supervisors.
- Submit required reports for technical, flagrant, administrative, spectator, facility, and unusual situations applicable to the track.
- Complete live-practicum observations and receive mentor/evaluator approval.
- Defend final portfolio before the RTBO advancement board.

## Month 1, Week 4: Communication Psychology
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NBA program is devoted to Communication Psychology. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of tone, timing, posture, coach dialogue, player dialogue, table communication, and emotional discipline. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NBA pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NBA official duties, Replay Center awareness, Coach’s Challenge administration, transition take foul awareness, professional restricted-area judgment, elite game flow, accuracy analytics, crew-chief accountability. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Communication Psychology affects the NBA environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

The instructional line for NBA Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance in Week 6 is that foul theory and contact classification must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to elite professional basketball officials preparing for NBA-style rule administration, Replay Center interaction, Coach’s Challenge procedures, professional crew hierarchy, and national-level performance analytics. The student is expected to understand that common fouls, shooting fouls, player-control, team-control, illegal contact, marginal contact, and contact that affects the play directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how NBA official duties, Replay Center awareness, Coach’s Challenge administration, transition take foul awareness influence the way this lesson appears in the NBA environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance, the student performs the day’s work as follows: Students perform the concept on the court through movement, positioning, whistle, signal, and crew-communication laboratories. For the NBA pathway, that performance must be connected to develop officials who think, prepare, communicate, and self-scout like elite professional basketball officials. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, personal fouls, flagrant fouls, away-from-the-play and transition take foul concepts, replay-triggered review issues, and league-office reporting discipline. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Foul Theory and Contact Classification. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

## Month 2, Week 7: Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy
### Weekly Professor's Opening Lecture
This week in the NBA program is devoted to Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy. The professor frames the week as a serious academic study of rhythm, speed, balance, quickness, displacement, freedom of movement, and game-flow judgment. Students are reminded that the purpose of this week is not to memorize a phrase but to transform the concept into repeatable officiating behavior. In the NBA pathway, the instructor repeatedly connects this material to NBA official duties, Replay Center awareness, Coach’s Challenge administration, transition take foul awareness, professional restricted-area judgment, elite game flow, accuracy analytics, crew-chief accountability. The student must leave the week able to explain the subject, perform it in a lab, identify it on film, communicate it in role-play, and apply it during practicum.

### Weekly Required Evidence
Students must produce a written journal entry, a film-lab worksheet, a court-lab rubric, a role-play score, and a mentor note showing how Advantage/Disadvantage Philosophy affects the NBA environment. If a student cannot produce evidence, the week is not complete.

The instructional line for NBA Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar in Week 14 is that post play, rebounding, and screening must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to elite professional basketball officials preparing for NBA-style rule administration, Replay Center interaction, Coach’s Challenge procedures, professional crew hierarchy, and national-level performance analytics. The student is expected to understand that post displacement, legal verticality, rebounding contact, illegal screens, off-ball coverage, and matchup awareness directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how NBA official duties, Replay Center awareness, Coach’s Challenge administration, transition take foul awareness influence the way this lesson appears in the NBA environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student performs the day’s work as follows: The professor introduces the week’s thesis, teaches the governing philosophy, questions the students orally, and requires every student to explain how the concept affects real officiating decisions. For the NBA pathway, that performance must be connected to develop officials who think, prepare, communicate, and self-scout like elite professional basketball officials. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, personal fouls, flagrant fouls, away-from-the-play and transition take foul concepts, replay-triggered review issues, and league-office reporting discipline. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 1 - Professor Lecture and Socratic Seminar, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Post Play, Rebounding, and Screening. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

The instructional line for NBA Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance in Week 32 is that level-specific reporting intensive must be studied as a professional officiating discipline rather than as a casual clinic topic. The professor begins by connecting the weekly subject to elite professional basketball officials preparing for NBA-style rule administration, Replay Center interaction, Coach’s Challenge procedures, professional crew hierarchy, and national-level performance analytics. The student is expected to understand that technical, flagrant, administrative, spectator, safety, and unusual-situation report writing for the track directly affects credibility, game control, fairness, safety, and advancement. This is not treated as an abstract discussion; it is taught as a working standard the official must demonstrate under pressure. The professor explains how NBA official duties, Replay Center awareness, Coach’s Challenge administration, transition take foul awareness influence the way this lesson appears in the NBA environment. Students must listen, take notes, ask disciplined questions, and prepare to defend how the concept applies to live action, crew communication, reporting, and assignment readiness. The classroom expectation is that every student can state the concept, explain why it matters, identify the risk of poor performance, and describe what professional behavior looks like before the course moves to the next activity.

#### Line Item 2 - What the Student Performs
The student performance task for this line requires active work, not passive attendance. During Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance, the student performs the day’s work as follows: Students perform the concept on the court through movement, positioning, whistle, signal, and crew-communication laboratories. For the NBA pathway, that performance must be connected to develop officials who think, prepare, communicate, and self-scout like elite professional basketball officials. The student writes notes in an officiating journal, identifies at least three practical game situations where the topic appears, and prepares one verbal explanation that could be delivered to a coach, partner, or supervisor. If the week involves contact or conduct, the student must also connect the lesson to technical fouls, personal fouls, flagrant fouls, away-from-the-play and transition take foul concepts, replay-triggered review issues, and league-office reporting discipline. If the week involves mechanics, the student must demonstrate where the official should stand, what the official should watch, and what visual angle is required. If the week involves communication, the student must perform the exact words, tone, posture, and stopping point that prevent over-explaining. This daily task is graded on preparation, specificity, professional vocabulary, and the ability to translate classroom theory into game behavior.

#### Line Item 3 - Expected Outcome, Evidence, and Grading
The expected outcome for this line is measurable. By the end of Day 3 - Court Laboratory and Mechanics Performance, the student should be able to demonstrate a clear improvement in understanding, language, positioning, judgment, or communication connected to Level-Specific Reporting Intensive. The professor or mentor records evidence through a written rubric, oral questioning, film worksheet, court-lab checklist, or live-practicum note. A passing student does not merely say that they understand the material; they proves understanding by applying it. For example, the student must identify the official’s primary coverage, explain the correct rule or philosophy, communicate the decision professionally, and describe the expected restart or report process when applicable. A student who cannot explain the concept clearly is assigned remediation before advancement. A student who performs the task well receives dashboard credit, mentor approval, and permission to continue toward higher-level assignments. The intended result is that knowledge becomes visible behavior, not unused information.

# FINAL CAPSTONE FOR NBA
The final capstone for NBA requires a complete officiating portfolio. The student submits full-year journals, rules exams, mechanics rubrics, film analysis, live observations, mentor notes, report-writing samples, communication role-play scores, and a personal advancement statement. During the final oral defense, the student must explain how they would manage a difficult game in the NBA environment, including pregame preparation, crew communication, contact philosophy, coach management, serious foul reporting, film self-scouting, and postgame professionalism. The board may ask the student to explain rules, justify a call/no-call, review a film clip, defend a report, or describe how they would handle a supervisor’s criticism. Passing the capstone earns RTBO Academy completion for this track and places the student into an assignment or advancement category based on demonstrated evidence.
